CPSP: Options on a fund of the largest US companies structured to protect against losses over the year starting each April, in exchange for a cap on gains. It is Calamos's defined protection design, meant for investors who want stock market exposure with the downside for the year largely removed.
DIVD: Dividend-paying companies from around the world, led by health care, banks and consumer staples, in a global value portfolio. It is an income holding that favors established payers across many countries, so it behaves more defensively than growth funds while still moving with world stock markets.
KEMQ: Internet and technology companies across emerging markets, including some privately held firms alongside listed ones, from KraneShares. Online shopping and consumer platforms dominate, making it a growth bet on the digital economies of China, Latin America and beyond, with extra risk from the private holdings.
QEW: The Nasdaq-100 spread evenly: every one of the hundred non-financial giants gets roughly the same weight instead of the biggest names dominating. Technology still leads at about 46 percent, but smaller members matter far more here, so it behaves a bit less like a big-tech fund.
GPT: Global large companies picked by an artificial intelligence system and held in equal weights, spread across technology, industry, health care and energy. It is a core worldwide holding where the stock selection comes from a machine model rather than human analysts, and no single giant dominates the mix.
PPTY: US real estate companies diversified deliberately across property types, from apartments and warehouses to shops, offices and data centers. The mix is set by property market fundamentals rather than company size, aiming for a more balanced property holding than the big-REIT-heavy indexes provide.
JANI: International stocks wrapped in options that buffer the first 15 percent of losses over the year starting each January, with a twist: gains are uncapped. Most buffer funds trade protection for a ceiling, so this one suits investors who want a cushion abroad without giving up the rally.
RNRG: Companies that produce power from renewable sources: wind, solar, hydro and geothermal generators, mostly regulated-style utilities worldwide. It is a steadier way into clean energy than panel or turbine makers, since these firms sell electricity under contract, though their shares still follow interest rates closely.
JXX: A concentrated portfolio of about twenty to thirty companies Janus Henderson managers believe can ride transformational changes, mostly large firms across technology, health care and industry. With so few holdings, each pick drives results, making it a high-conviction growth holding rather than a diversified core.
FDRV: Global companies building electric vehicles and future transportation: carmakers, battery and chip suppliers, charging and self-driving technology. It is a growth bet on the transport shift away from gasoline, concentrated in consumer and technology names, and it swings with the EV industry's fast-changing fortunes.
ACSV: Small US companies bought at value prices, chosen by American Century managers combining hands-on fundamental research with systematic, risk-aware construction. Banks lead at about 29 percent, and the design aims for a steadier small value holding than the rough-and-tumble small-cap indexes usually deliver.
BCDF: Companies developing blockchain technology and digital asset businesses, from crypto exchanges and financial firms to miners and tech suppliers, actively picked worldwide. It is Horizon Kinetics' stock-based route into crypto's growth, volatile like the industry but holding businesses rather than coins themselves.
SIFI: A systematic income portfolio run with Ares, a major credit manager, spanning many bond sectors and using derivatives like credit default swaps and Treasury futures. It applies institutional credit machinery to a multisector income role, shifting exposures by model rather than by a single manager's hunches.
TIZE: Securitized debt picked by TCW specialists: bonds backed by mortgages and other loan pools, many issued or guaranteed by US government agencies. It is an income holding built on housing and consumer credit, where loan-level analysis matters more than picking between famous corporate borrowers.
FTXG: US food and beverage companies selected from the Nasdaq by liquidity: packaged food makers, drink companies and producers that fill supermarket shelves. It is a defensive consumer staples bet, the kind of steady, everyday-spending industry that usually holds up better when the economy and markets wobble.
QQQS: The next generation of Nasdaq companies: about two hundred smaller listed firms not in the Nasdaq-100, with health care over half thanks to young biotech and medical firms. It is a growth bet on tomorrow's Nasdaq names before they graduate, and small biotech makes it extra volatile.
LDRH: A ladder of iShares term bond funds holding high yield and other income corporate bonds maturing across the next one to five years. Spreading end dates smooths the ride versus a single-year fund, paying junk bond interest while each rung matures and rolls into new bonds.
FPAA: A global allocation portfolio from FPA's value-minded managers, holding about 61 percent stocks and 36 percent bonds worldwide, partly through other funds. It is a one-stop moderate portfolio run with a contrarian, bargain-hunting style, so its mix can drift from the usual balanced fund template.
MJSC: Small Japanese companies actively picked by MUFG managers, led by industrial firms, then technology, banks and consumer businesses. It is a focused bet on Japan's smaller domestic companies, a segment global investors often overlook, with the yen's moves adding to results for US holders.
ROPE: One hundred actively chosen US stocks with a defensive escape hatch: the managers can move up to everything into cash when conditions look dangerous. It aims to join stock gains in good times and dodge deep falls in bad ones, so its success depends on the managers' timing calls.
DUKH: A tactical rotation among high income bond funds, long-term Treasury funds and cash, run by Ocean Park's risk-managed process. It chases high yield when trends are friendly and shelters in Treasuries or cash when they are not, making income the goal but capital protection the governor.
DDTD: An options structure on the largest US companies designed to gain in either direction: it can profit from a modest rise or a modest fall over its year from December, while buffering the first 10 percent of losses. Deep moves either way can still hurt, and gains are capped.
AIED: Large US stocks chosen by a momentum model driven by a large language model that scans for catalysts like earnings news and analyst shifts. Technology dominates at about 72 percent, and the AI-run selection makes it a fast-moving growth holding that can change its lineup as the news flow changes.
AWAY: Travel technology companies worldwide: online booking platforms, reservation software and the digital plumbing behind trips. It is a growth bet on how travel is bought and managed rather than on airlines or hotels themselves, so it rides global travel demand with a technology twist.
INVG: US investment grade corporate bonds chosen by GMO's systematic process, scoring each bond on value, quality and other factors. It is a core corporate bond holding with a rules-driven twist, aiming to own the attractively priced, sound credits a plain index weights only by size.
GOLI: Income built on gold: Treasury-style holdings plus options giving indirect exposure to the big gold fund's share price, with gains on that exposure limited by design. It aims to turn gold's moves into regular payments, so it pays more like an income fund than a pure metal bet.
BEMD: Bonds from emerging market governments and companies, in a BNY Mellon portfolio spanning the developing world's debt. It pays higher interest than developed market bonds, and returns hinge on those countries' finances and currencies, so it belongs on the riskier side of a bond allocation.
XIDE: Options on a fund of the largest US companies plus short-term Treasury securities combine two aims over the period from December: a buffer against a slice of stock losses and a stream of premium income. It is built for investors who want equity exposure with built-in cushioning and regular payouts.
KONG: Large and midsize US companies with fortress-like qualities: strong balance sheets, durable positions and steady cash generation, across technology, industry and health care. It is a quality-first core holding that favors companies built to survive storms, accepting it may trail flashier stocks in strong rallies.
ICPI: Inflation-protected Treasury bonds with under a year to maturity, the shortest-dated corner of the TIPS market. It barely moves with interest rates, so it works as a cash-like parking place whose value adjusts with inflation, aimed at preserving purchasing power over short horizons.
JMID: Midsize US growth companies picked by Janus Henderson with an active, systematic process hunting for an edge in that middle tier. Technology, industry, consumer and health care names share the lead, making it a diversified growth holding focused on companies past the fragile stage but not yet giants.
BDVG: US companies that pay and grow dividends, selected with a Berkshire-inspired discipline emphasizing durable businesses and shareholder returns. It is a value-leaning income and growth holding: dividends are central, but the managers look for payers whose dividends should keep rising rather than the highest yields today.
RDYY: A single-stock income strategy built on Reddit shares, using options on that one social media company to generate regular payments. Because everything rides on one young, volatile company plus the options overlay, it is highly concentrated: income can be generous, but gains are capped and drops hit directly.
VMSD: Short-duration municipal bonds from states, counties and cities across the US, paying interest exempt from regular federal income tax. Short maturities keep price swings small, so it is a cautious tax-free income holding, a step up in yield from a money market fund for taxed investors.
PSCD: Small US consumer discretionary companies: the retailers, restaurants, car-related and leisure firms selling things people buy when they feel flush. It is a focused bet on the American consumer's mood, and small discretionary stocks are among the first to fall when shoppers pull back.
HDG: Financial instruments engineered to copy the overall returns of the hedge fund industry, using liquid positions rather than actual hedge funds. It aims to deliver that alternative return pattern, steadier and less tied to stocks, inside an ordinary fund, though replication is approximate and cash collateral does much of the work.
USSH: US Treasury bonds laddered across one to three year maturities, so some bonds are always near maturity and reinvesting at current rates. It is a conservative income holding for money needed soon, with minimal credit risk and modest price movement when interest rates shift.
VMHY: High yield municipal bonds: below-investment-grade and unrated debt from cities, hospitals and projects paying the richest tax-exempt interest available. It is the aggressive end of tax-free income, and the weaker credits mean bigger falls than quality muni funds when investors worry about defaults.
QUSA: Quality US companies, heavy in technology, paired with an options program built to pay a targeted level of monthly income, the 15 in its name. It aims to pair sturdy stock holdings with unusually high cash distributions, giving up some stock gains to keep the payments flowing.
WBIF: US and foreign stocks of all sizes picked for value by WBI managers, with a large cash cushion of about 27 percent that shifts with their outlook. It is a tactical value holding aiming for growth with an eye on protection, so its results rest heavily on the managers' market calls.
BRF: Small Brazilian companies across consumer, materials, industrial and property sectors, in a single-country fund. Small caps in Brazil swing hard with the real, local politics and commodity cycles, making this one of the most volatile ways to bet on Latin America's biggest economy.
XOEF: The big US index with its hundred largest members removed, leaving the roughly four hundred other large companies in more even measure. Technology shrinks to about 22 percent, so it is a core holding for investors who find the usual index too concentrated in mega-cap giants.
TMNS: Short-term municipal bonds paying interest exempt from regular federal income tax, actively managed for stability and income. It is a conservative tax-free holding for money with a near-term purpose, keeping maturities short so its price barely moves when interest rates change.
MEMS: Small companies across emerging markets, actively hunted by Matthews Asia specialists who look for undiscovered growers country by country. Industrials, technology and banks lead the mix, and the discovery approach means owning names most emerging market index funds have barely noticed yet.
XLKI: Technology stocks, the full sector from chipmakers to software giants, paired with an options program that collects premium income on top. It aims for sector returns plus extra income with a slightly smoother ride, giving up some upside when technology shares climb quickly.
RISE: Emerging market stocks chosen by Pictet managers in what they call rising economies, with banks about a third, plus materials, technology and consumer firms. It is a developing markets holding from a Swiss active shop, spread across regions rather than dominated by the usual Asian giants.
ANTW: Companies in the ecosystem of Anthropic, the AI lab: its cloud partners, backers, suppliers and customers most exposed to its technology. Technology and finance names lead, and it is an unusually narrow theme, a bet on one AI company's orbit rather than the whole artificial intelligence field.
APXM: Options referencing a fund of the largest US companies aim for the maximum available buffer against losses over a one-year outcome period starting each April. In exchange for that deeper protection, the cap on gains is lower than on lighter buffer funds, so it is the cautious end of the range.
VAVX: A single-cryptocurrency trust holding AVAX, the token of the Avalanche blockchain network, valued daily against a published benchmark rate. It gives brokerage-account access to that one digital asset without a crypto wallet, and it swings as sharply as the token itself.
BSJX: High yield corporate bonds that all mature in 2033, in an Invesco BulletShares fund with a set end date. It works like a ladder rung for a 2033 goal, paying junk bond interest while defaults remain the key risk, and its price swings fade as the end approaches.
